# Respirometry {.unnumbered}

Authors: Nicholas Wu

Estimating metabolic rate from raw oxygen traces with a structured, reproducible 
workflow following the [`respR`](https://januarharianto.github.io/respR/) R package 
[@Harianto2019].

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Workshop overview

**By the end of this workshop you will be able to:**

1. Recognise common problems in raw oxygen traces before they bias your results.
2. Import, quality check, extract, background-correct and convert oxygen uptake
   rates with the [`respR`](https://januarharianto.github.io/respR/) package
   [@Harianto2019] in a `tidyverse` workflow.
3. Adapt the same workflow to **aerial** (gas-phase) respirometry.
4. Report your workflow so it can be reproduced and synthesised by others.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center", comment = "#>")
```

## Background {.unnumbered}

### Why measure oxygen? {.unnumbered}

Metabolic rate (MR), the rate at which an organism uses energy, underpins
almost every question in thermal ecology: how much energy an animal needs at a
given temperature, how much it has left for growth and reproduction, and how
close it is to its physiological limits. Because aerobic metabolism consumes
oxygen in near-fixed proportion to the energy released, the most common way to
estimate MR is **indirect calorimetry**: measuring the rate of oxygen
consumption ($\dot{M}\text{O}_2$ in water breathers, $\dot{V}\text{O}_2$ in air
breathers) and/or carbon dioxide production [@Lighton2019; @Wu2024].

Depending on the state of the animal, the rate is interpreted as a different
**metabolic rate metric**:

| Metric | Definition (short) |
|----|----|
| Standard metabolic rate (SMR) | MR of an inactive, unstressed, post-absorptive adult **ectotherm** in its inactive phase [@Chabot2016; @Wu2024] |
| Basal metabolic rate (BMR) | The **endotherm** equivalent of SMR, measured within the thermoneutral zone [@Wu2024] |
| Resting / routine metabolic rate (RMR) | MR of a resting animal when one or more SMR/BMR conditions cannot be met; *routine* MR includes spontaneous activity [@Killen2021; @Wu2024] |
| Maximum metabolic rate (MMR) | Maximum aerobic O~2~ uptake, e.g. during or immediately after exhaustive exercise [@Killen2021] |
| Aerobic scope | MMR − SMR (absolute) or MMR / SMR (factorial) [@Clark2013] |

### Types of respirometry {.unnumbered}

All respirometry methods record oxygen over time; they differ in how oxygen is
supplied to the animal (@fig-resp-methods).

![Four common respirometry designs and the idealised oxygen traces they produce. In closed and intermittent-flow systems the metabolic rate is proportional to the **slope** of oxygen against time; in flow-through systems it is proportional to the **difference** between inflow and outflow oxygen multiplied by the flow rate; in an aerial closed system the slope of O~2~ partial pressure is converted to moles with the gas law.](images/resp_methods.svg){#fig-resp-methods fig-alt="Schematic of closed, intermittent-flow, flow-through and aerial closed-system respirometers with idealised oxygen traces." width="100%"}

For **closed** and **intermittent-flow** respirometry, the oxygen uptake rate is

$$
\dot{M}\text{O}_2 = -\left(\beta_{\text{animal}} - \beta_{\text{blank}}\right) \times V_{\text{eff}}
$$

where $\beta$ is the slope of a linear regression of oxygen concentration
against time for the animal chamber and for an empty ("blank") chamber that
measures background (microbial) oxygen use, and $V_{\text{eff}}$ is the
*effective* volume of water (respirometer + tubing − animal volume)
[@Steffensen1989; @Svendsen2016]. For **flow-through** respirometry,
$\dot{M}\text{O}_2 = (C_{\text{in}} - C_{\text{out}}) \times FR$, where $FR$ is
the flow rate [@Lighton2019].

### Why a structured, reproducible workflow? {.unnumbered}

Turning a raw oxygen trace into a single number involves many decisions:
which part of the trace to use, how long the regression window is, how to
correct for background, which volume and which units. Each decision can change
the final value, and most are never reported. A survey of 202 aquatic intermittent-flow respirometry papers found reporting to be poor and inconsistent: only 71% clearly 
stated body mass at the time of measurement, 34% how many measurements were used 
to estimate SMR, and more than 30% did not mention background respiration at all 
[@Killen2021].

Analytical choices alone matter, where BMR estimates can be 12–30% higher when 
calculated from 10–15 min windows rather than 60 min windows [@Hayes1992; @Jacobs2014], 
shorter regression windows inflate MMR [@Prinzing2021], and filtering slopes by a 
high r^2^ threshold can bias SMR upward [@Chabot2021].

Manually selecting regions in a spreadsheet makes these decisions invisible and
impossible to audit. A **scripted, object-based workflow** records every
parameter alongside the result, reduces transcription and unit-conversion
errors, and lets a reviewer or meta-analyst rerun the analysis from raw data
[@Harianto2019; @Wu2024]. Both the aquatic [@Killen2021] and terrestrial
[@Wu2024] reporting guidelines recommend open-source, command-line tools such as
`respR` [@Harianto2019] or `LoLinR` [@Olito2017] for exactly this reason.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Reproducibility vs. replicability

**Reproducibility** = getting the same result from the *same data and code*.
**Replicability** = getting consistent results from a *new study* asking the same
question. A scripted workflow guarantees the first and makes the second
possible, because others can copy your exact methods [@Wu2024].
:::

## Common problems {.unnumbered}

### Problems in the raw data {.unnumbered}

| Problem | What it looks like | Why it matters | Where `respR` helps |
|----|----|----|----|
| Non-numeric, missing (`NA`), infinite, duplicated or out-of-order time values | Import errors, gaps, sensor drop-outs | Regressions fail or silently use the wrong rows | `inspect()` |
| Initial disturbance | Steep or curved section at the start | Handling stress, thermal and mixing equilibration inflate rates | `inspect()`, `subset_data()`, `calc_rate(from, to)` |
| Sensor interference / spikes | Sudden drops or jumps | One artefact can dominate a regression | `inspect()` rolling-rate plot |
| Activity bursts | Short steep sections | Fine for MMR, wrong for SMR/RMR | `auto_rate()` methods |
| Flush periods | Saw-tooth oxygen rises | Must be excluded from rate windows | `calc_rate.int()`, `auto_rate.int()` |
| Very low oxygen | Curvature as O~2~ falls | Animals may change behaviour or become O~2~-conformers | `calc_rate(by = "oxygen")`, `oxy_crit()` |
| Background respiration or sensor drift | Slow decline in a blank chamber | Animal rate is overestimated | `calc_rate.bg()`, `adjust_rate()` |
| Wrong volume or units | Rates orders of magnitude off | Classic source of published errors | `convert_rate()`, `convert_MR()` |

Here are some real examples from the data that come with `respR` (we load the
packages properly in the next section).

```{r}
#| label: fig-resp-problems
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Common problems in raw oxygen traces, all from datasets supplied with `respR`. (A) unstable start; (B) a sensor artefact mid-trial; (C) irregularities near the end; (D) flushes in an intermittent-flow trial."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| 
library(tidyverse)
library(respR)

problem_traces <- bind_rows(
  urchins.rd |> as_tibble() |>
    transmute(time = time.min, o2 = b, panel = "A. Initial disturbance (urchins.rd, b)"),
  urchins.rd |> as_tibble() |>
    transmute(time = time.min, o2 = h, panel = "B. Sensor interference (urchins.rd, h)"),
  urchins.rd |> as_tibble() |>
    transmute(time = time.min, o2 = n, panel = "C. Irregular end of trial (urchins.rd, n)"),
  intermittent.rd |> as_tibble() |>
    transmute(time = Time / 60, o2 = O2, panel = "D. Flush periods (intermittent.rd)")
)

ggplot(problem_traces, aes(x = time, y = o2)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Time (min)", y = expression(O[2]~"(mg L"^-1*")")) +
  theme_bw()
```


## Example Workflow {.unnumbered}

At minimum, your raw data need:

- a **numeric time** column (e.g. seconds or minutes since the start), and
- one or more **oxygen** columns (any unit).

Everything up to the conversion step in `respR` is unitless, so it works for
water or air, for uptake or production. Metadata you will need at the
conversion step: oxygen and time units, effective volume, specimen mass, and
(for some units) temperature, salinity and atmospheric pressure.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Run once to install
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "respR"))
```

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load libraries
library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and plotting
library(respR)     # respirometry processing
```

The workflow we will follow is shown as below. Each `respR`
function returns an object that the next function understands, so the
parameters of every step travel with the result.


::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills}

# Aquatic Respirometry {.unnumbered}

We will analyse `urchins.rd`, a closed-chamber experiment on the sea urchin
*Heliocidaris erythrogramma* [@Carey2016] that is supplied with [`respR`](https://januarharianto.github.io/respR/). It
contains time in **minutes**, dissolved oxygen in **mg L^-1^** for 16 urchins
(columns `a` to `p`), and two blank chambers (`b1`, `b2`). The experiment was
run at 20 °C, salinity 30 and 1.01 bar in 1.09 L respirometers.

The tutorial will use data from a close-chamber respiromety experiment, but the 
package is able to handle intermittent-flow and open-flow respirometry, and 
critical oxygen values (P~crit~).

## Import {.unnumbered}

The data are already in R. For your own files you would use `read_csv()`
(see the aerial example below). It is good practice to store the experimental
metadata in one place rather than typing numbers into later functions.

```{r}
urchins <- as_tibble(urchins.rd)
urchins

# Metadata for the experiment (from ?urchins.rd)
urchin_meta <- list(
  oxy_unit  = "mg/L",
  time_unit = "min",
  volume_L  = 1.09,  # effective volume of water (L)
  temp_C    = 20,
  sal       = 30,
  pres_bar  = 1.01,
  mass_kg   = 0.19   # example specimen mass used in the respR vignette
)
```

A quick tidy plot of every chamber is the fastest way to spot problems.

```{r}
#| label: fig-urchins-all
#| fig-cap: "Oxygen traces of 16 urchins and two blank chambers."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
urchins |>
  pivot_longer(-time.min, names_to = "chamber", values_to = "o2_mgL") |>
  mutate(type = if_else(chamber %in% c("b1", "b2"), "Blank", "Urchin")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time.min, y = o2_mgL, colour = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ chamber, ncol = 6, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Blank = "#2b6cb0", Urchin = "black")) +
  labs(x = "Time (min)", y = expression(O[2]~"(mg L"^-1*")"), colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Quality check {.unnumbered}

`inspect()` checks that the time and oxygen columns are numeric, finite, free of
`NA`s, sequential, not duplicated and evenly spaced, and plots the data with a
rolling rate.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
inspect(urchins, time = 1, oxygen = 2:19)
```

The only warning is that time is not evenly spaced. That is expected here
(decimal minutes are rounded to 0.1 or 0.2 min), and `respR` uses actual time
values, so it is safe. Now inspect a single urchin and save the result:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
urchin <- inspect(urchins, time = "time.min", oxygen = "n")
```

The bottom panel (rolling rate across 10% of the data) shows a stable rate of
about −0.02 mg L^-1^ min^-1^ for the first ~29 minutes, after which the trace
becomes irregular (the urchin interfered with the sensor). A regression across
the whole trace would not represent routine metabolism.

## Calculate O~2~ uptake rate {.unnumbered}

### Manual selection with `calc_rate()` {.unnumbered}

Without extra arguments, `calc_rate()` fits a regression to the whole dataset (see 
below).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
calc_rate(urchin)                           # whole trace (not appropriate here)
```

Use `from`, `to` and `by` (`"time"`, `"row"` or `"oxygen"`) to choose a region. 
In this case, from 4 to 29 time points.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
urch_rate <- calc_rate(urchin, from = 4, to = 29, by = "time")
```

Show summary of the rate with the `summary()` function.

```{r}
summary(urch_rate)
```

Note the **negative** rate: in `respR`, oxygen *uptake* is a negative slope.
The r^2^ of `r round(urch_rate$summary$rsq, 3)` indicates a good linear fit.

### Objective selection with `auto_rate()` {.unnumbered}

Hand-picking a window is subjective. `auto_rate()` runs rolling regressions and,
with the default `method = "linear"`, uses kernel density estimation to find the
most consistently linear regions. Other methods return the `"lowest"` or
`"highest"` rates for a given window width (useful for SMR and MMR).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
urch_auto <- auto_rate(urchin)
```

```{r}
summary(urch_auto)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`auto_rate()` is a tool, **not an oracle**. Always look at the plot and the summary,
and check that the regions it chooses make biological sense (e.g. not right
after handling, not during an artefact).
:::

## Background O~2~ rate {.unnumbered}

Microbes in the water also consume oxygen. Blank chambers run under identical
conditions estimate this background rate. `calc_rate.bg()` calculates the rate
in one or more blank columns.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
bg_rate <- calc_rate.bg(urchins, time = 1, oxygen = 18:19)
bg_rate
```

Then subtract it from the specimen rate with `adjust_rate()`. The default
`method = "mean"` uses the mean of the two blanks. (For backgrounds that change
over a long experiment, see the `"linear"`, `"exponential"` and `"paired"`
methods in `?adjust_rate`.)

```{r}
urch_rate_adj <- adjust_rate(urch_rate, by = bg_rate, method = "mean")
```

::: {.callout-note}
Background was `r round(abs(bg_rate$rate.bg.mean / urch_rate$rate) * 100, 1)`%
of the urchin's uptake here. Background typically grows over a long experiment
(biofilm), so measure it at the start **and** end, and report how it was
applied [@Killen2021].
:::

## Conversions {.unnumbered}

Until now nothing has had units. `convert_rate()` needs the units of the raw
data, the effective volume (L), and optionally mass (kg) or area (m^2^). Some
oxygen units (e.g. `%Air`, `mL/L`) also need temperature (`t`), salinity (`S`)
and pressure (`P`, bar).

```{r}
# Absolute rate: whole-animal mg O2 per hour
convert_rate(urch_rate_adj,
             oxy.unit    = urchin_meta$oxy_unit,
             time.unit   = urchin_meta$time_unit,
             output.unit = "mg/h",
             volume      = urchin_meta$volume_L)
```

```{r}
# Mass-specific rate, saved as the final object
urch_rate_final <- convert_rate(urch_rate_adj,
                                oxy.unit    = urchin_meta$oxy_unit,
                                time.unit   = urchin_meta$time_unit,
                                output.unit = "mL/h/kg",
                                volume      = urchin_meta$volume_L,
                                mass        = urchin_meta$mass_kg,
                                t = urchin_meta$temp_C,
                                S = urchin_meta$sal,
                                P = urchin_meta$pres_bar)
urch_rate_final
```

Use `unit_args()` to see every unit `respR` understands. Units are matched
flexibly, so `"mg/L"`, `"mg l-1"` and `"mg per litre"` are equivalent.

::: {.callout-important}
The `volume` is the volume of **water**, not of the respirometer. Subtract the
animal's volume (for most aquatic animals, mass in kg ≈ volume in L) and add the
volume of any recirculation tubing.
:::

## Final O~2~ uptake rate {.unnumbered}

`summary(..., export = TRUE)` returns a data frame with every parameter used:
the regression window, r^2^, background, units, volume, mass and the final rate.
This one row is your **analysis record**.

```{r}
#| results: hide
urch_final_df <- summary(urch_rate_final, export = TRUE) |> as_tibble()
```

```{r}
urch_final_df |>
  select(time, endtime, rsq, rate, adjustment, rate.adjusted,
         volume, mass, rate.output, output.unit)
```

**Sanity-check the result.** A misplaced decimal or wrong unit is easy to miss,
so compare your value with published rates of similar species, sizes and
temperatures. `convert_MR()` converts between metabolic rate units:

```{r}
convert_MR(urch_rate_final, to = "umol/h/g",
           t = urchin_meta$temp_C, S = urchin_meta$sal, P = urchin_meta$pres_bar)
```

The `respR` closed-chamber vignette compares this value with published sea
urchin rates of roughly 0.2–0.6 µmol O~2~ h^-1^ g^-1^ at 22–25 °C, so the result
is in the right ballpark.

### The whole workflow in one pipe {.unnumbered}

Because each function passes its object to the next, the entire analysis is a
few readable lines, which is exactly what you would archive alongside the raw
data:

```{r}
#| results: hide
#| fig-show: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false
urchin_n_result <- urchins |>
  inspect(time = "time.min", oxygen = "n") |>
  calc_rate(from = 4, to = 29, by = "time") |>
  adjust_rate(by = calc_rate.bg(urchins, time = 1, oxygen = 18:19)) |>
  convert_rate(oxy.unit = "mg/L", time.unit = "min",
               output.unit = "mL/h/kg", volume = 1.09, mass = 0.19,
               t = 20, S = 30, P = 1.01) |>
  summary(export = TRUE)
```


# Aerial Respirometry

`respR` was designed for aquatic respirometry, but its rate functions are
unitless, so the same `inspect()` → `calc_rate()` → `adjust_rate()` →
`convert_rate()` chain works for **air**. The key difference is the
conversion from the oxygen signal to an amount of oxygen.

::: {.callout-important}
## Do not use `respR`'s pressure or %-saturation units for air

`respR` conversions of `"%Air"`, `"%Oxy"`, `"hPa"`, `"kPa"`, `"Torr"` and similar
units use the **solubility of oxygen in water**. In air, a given partial
pressure contains about 30 times more oxygen per litre than water at the same
partial pressure. For gas-phase data, convert partial pressure to a molar
concentration yourself with the ideal gas law, then give `respR` a unit that
does not depend on solubility (e.g. `"umol/L"`).
:::

For a sealed, rigid chamber at constant temperature, the oxygen concentration in
the air is

$$
C_{\text{O}_2} = \frac{p\text{O}_2}{R\,T}
$$

where $p\text{O}_2$ is the oxygen partial pressure (Pa), $R$ = 8.314 J mol^-1^
K^-1^ and $T$ is temperature (K). With $p\text{O}_2$ in hPa,
$C_{\text{O}_2}$ (µmol L^-1^) $= p\text{O}_2 \times 10^5 / (R\,T)$. The uptake rate
is then the slope of $C_{\text{O}_2}$ against time multiplied by the **air**
volume (chamber volume − animal volume). Because moles of oxygen are counted
directly from the partial pressure, CO~2~ accumulating in the chamber does not
dilute the signal, and the result can be expressed as a gas volume at standard
temperature and pressure (STPD: 0 °C, 101.325 kPa; 1 mol ≈ 22.414 L)
[@Lighton2019].

::: {.callout-note}
The example data below are **simulated** for teaching (see
`data/simulate_resp_aerial.py` in the book repository): a 4.2 g lizard in a
150 mL glass chamber at 25 °C, with an optical oxygen sensor reading $p\text{O}_2$
(hPa) every 10 s for 100 min, plus an empty blank chamber run in parallel. The
true resting uptake used in the simulation is 22.5 µmol O~2~ h^-1^, so you can
check how close the workflow gets.
:::

## Import {.unnumbered}

Instrument exports typically have metadata lines at the top, column names with
spaces and units, and separate date and time columns. Read the file, then
rename columns and build a numeric time column.

```{r}
#| message: false
# Use the local copy if you cloned the repository, otherwise read from GitHub
aerial_file <- "data/resp_aerial_lizard.csv"
if (!file.exists(aerial_file)) {
  aerial_file <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nicholaswunz/thermal_ecology_R/refs/heads/main/data/resp_aerial_lizard.csv"
}

aerial_raw <- read_csv(aerial_file,
                       comment = "#",                 # skip metadata lines
                       na = c("", "NA", "NaN"),       # sensor drop-outs
                       show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(aerial_raw)
```

```{r}
aerial <- aerial_raw |>
  rename(date         = Date,
         clock        = Time,
         dt_s         = `dt (s)`,
         o2_spec_hpa  = `Ch1 Oxygen (hPa)`,
         o2_blank_hpa = `Ch2 Oxygen (hPa)`,
         temp_c       = `Temp (degC)`,
         baro_hpa     = `Pressure (hPa)`) |>
  mutate(date_time = dmy_hms(paste(date, clock)),
         time_min  = as.numeric(difftime(date_time, first(date_time),
                                         units = "mins")))

aerial_meta <- list(
  chamber_L = 0.150,
  mass_g    = 4.2,
  air_L     = 0.150 - 4.2 / 1000  # chamber minus animal volume (density ~1 g/mL)
)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
`respR::format_time()` is an alternative way to turn date-time strings into
numeric time (in seconds from the first value).
:::

## Quality check {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
inspect(aerial, time = "time_min", oxygen = c("o2_spec_hpa", "o2_blank_hpa"))
```

`inspect()` reports `NA` values in the specimen channel (two sensor drop-outs)
and uneven time spacing (a 1-min logger pause near 70 min). Neither biases a
regression on real time values once the `NA`s are removed. Also check the
environmental columns: a sealed chamber is only valid if temperature is stable.

```{r}
aerial |>
  summarise(across(c(temp_c, baro_hpa),
                   list(mean = mean, min = min, max = max)))
```

```{r}
aerial_clean <- aerial |>
  drop_na(o2_spec_hpa)
```

## Convert partial pressure to concentration {.unnumbered}

```{r}
R_gas <- 8.314462618  # J mol-1 K-1

aerial_clean <- aerial_clean |>
  mutate(temp_K        = temp_c + 273.15,
         o2_spec_umol  = o2_spec_hpa  * 1e5 / (R_gas * temp_K),  # umol O2 per L air
         o2_blank_umol = o2_blank_hpa * 1e5 / (R_gas * temp_K))
```

## Calculate O~2~ uptake rate {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
spec_insp <- inspect(aerial_clean, time = "time_min", oxygen = "o2_spec_umol")
```

The rolling rate shows elevated uptake for the first ~8 min (handling), a burst
of activity around 40–47 min, and stable resting uptake elsewhere. For a
resting rate, use a window after settling and before the activity:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
spec_rate <- calc_rate(spec_insp, from = 10, to = 40, by = "time")
```

## Background O~2~ rate {.unnumbered}

In air there is little microbial respiration, but blanks still capture sensor
drift, small leaks and respiration of any substrate in the chamber.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
blank_insp <- inspect(aerial_clean, time = "time_min", oxygen = "o2_blank_umol",
                      plot = FALSE)
blank_rate <- calc_rate.bg(blank_insp)

spec_rate_adj <- adjust_rate(spec_rate, by = blank_rate)
```

## Conversions {.unnumbered}

Because the data are now in µmol L^-1^, `convert_rate()` needs no temperature,
salinity or pressure, and the `volume` is the **air** volume.

```{r}
#| message: false
aerial_final <- convert_rate(spec_rate_adj,
                             oxy.unit    = "umol/L",
                             time.unit   = "min",
                             output.unit = "umol/h",
                             volume      = aerial_meta$air_L)

aerial_final_mass <- convert_rate(spec_rate_adj,
                                  oxy.unit    = "umol/L",
                                  time.unit   = "min",
                                  output.unit = "umol/h/g",
                                  volume      = aerial_meta$air_L,
                                  mass        = aerial_meta$mass_g / 1000)  # kg
```

## Final O~2~ consumption {.unnumbered}

Terrestrial studies usually report $\dot{V}\text{O}_2$ as mL O~2~ h^-1^ at STPD.

```{r}
aerial_result <- tibble(
  umol_h      = abs(aerial_final$rate.output),
  umol_h_g    = abs(aerial_final_mass$rate.output),
  mL_h_STPD   = umol_h * 22.414 / 1000,
  mL_h_g_STPD = umol_h_g * 22.414 / 1000
)
aerial_result
```

The workflow recovers `r round(aerial_result$umol_h, 1)` µmol O~2~ h^-1^,
close to the true value of 22.5 µmol h^-1^ used in the simulation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Going further: flow-through aerial respirometry

Most terrestrial work uses **flow-through** (open-flow) respirometry, where air
flows through the chamber at a known rate and O~2~ is measured as a *fractional*
concentration. The equation depends on where the flow is measured and which
gases are scrubbed. The standard equation, for flow ($\dot{V}_I$) measured
*before* the chamber with CO~2~ and water vapour removed before the O~2~
analyser, is [@Withers2001]:

$$
\dot{V}\text{O}_2 = \frac{\dot{V}_I\,(F_I\text{O}_2 - F_E\text{O}_2)}{1 - F_E\text{O}_2}
$$

If CO~2~ is *not* removed from the excurrent air, using this equation
overestimates $\dot{V}\text{O}_2$ by about 21% in Withers' worked example, and
other flow-meter positions need different equations [@Withers2001]. Flow-through
data also need baseline drift and lag corrections [@Lighton2011; @Lighton2019].
`respR` is not designed for these corrections, so whatever tool you use for
aerial flow-through data, state exactly which equation was applied. For closed
systems where gas *fractions* are measured from syringe samples, the dilution
and CO~2~ corrections of @Vleck1987 apply.
:::

:::

# Activities {.unnumbered}

::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills}

# Aquatic {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 1: Inspect before you analyse

Inspect urchin `h` with `inspect()`. (a) What problem do you see, and roughly
when does it occur? (b) Which time window(s) would you use to estimate its
routine metabolic rate?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 1

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
urchin_h <- inspect(urchins, time = "time.min", oxygen = "h")
```

(a) Oxygen drops sharply between about 22 and 30 min and then jumps back up,
which is physically impossible for a sealed chamber. It is a sensor artefact
(e.g. the urchin covering the sensor spot), not respiration.

(b) Any window clear of the artefact, for example 2–20 min (after the start-up
period) or 31–45 min. The earlier window is longer and starts after handling,
so it is a sensible choice.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 2: Why you must not apply one window to every chamber

Calculate the rate of urchin `h` (a) over the whole trace, (b) using the same
4–29 min window we used for urchin `n`, and (c) over 2–20 min. Compare the rates
and r^2^ values. Which is correct, and why are the other two wrong?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 2

```{r}
#| fig-show: hide
#| results: hide
h_whole <- calc_rate(urchin_h)
h_4_29  <- calc_rate(urchin_h, from = 4, to = 29, by = "time")
h_2_20  <- calc_rate(urchin_h, from = 2, to = 20, by = "time")
```

```{r}
tibble(window = c("whole trace", "4-29 min", "2-20 min"),
       rate   = c(h_whole$rate, h_4_29$rate, h_2_20$rate),
       rsq    = c(h_whole$summary$rsq, h_4_29$summary$rsq, h_2_20$summary$rsq))
```

The 2–20 min window gives the valid estimate (high r^2^, no artefact). The 4–29
min window *includes* the artefact and overestimates uptake by roughly
`r round((h_4_29$rate / h_2_20$rate - 1) * 100)`%; the whole-trace regression is
pulled the other way by the post-artefact jump. A window that is right for one
chamber can be badly wrong for another, so inspect every trace.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 3: Scale up with the tidyverse

Use `purrr::map()` to process all 16 urchins with the same pipeline
(`inspect()` → `calc_rate()` from 4 to 29 min → `adjust_rate()` with `bg_rate`
→ `convert_rate()` to mg h^-1^) and collect the results in one tibble. Which
urchin would an r^2^ ≥ 0.95 filter flag, and why does that matter?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 3

```{r}
#| results: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false
urchin_rates <- tibble(chamber = letters[1:16]) |>
  mutate(
    insp = map(chamber, \(x) inspect(urchins, time = "time.min",
                                     oxygen = x, plot = FALSE)),
    rate = map(insp, \(x) calc_rate(x, from = 4, to = 29, by = "time",
                                    plot = FALSE)),
    adj  = map(rate, \(x) adjust_rate(x, by = bg_rate)),
    conv = map(adj, \(x) convert_rate(x, oxy.unit = "mg/L", time.unit = "min",
                                      output.unit = "mg/h", volume = 1.09)),
    res  = map(conv, \(x) summary(x, export = TRUE))
  ) |>
  select(chamber, res) |>
  unnest(res)
```

```{r}
urchin_rates |>
  select(chamber, rsq, rate.adjusted, rate.output, output.unit) |>
  mutate(flag = if_else(rsq < 0.95, "check trace!", ""))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
urchin_rates |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(chamber, abs(rate.output)), y = abs(rate.output),
             fill = rsq < 0.95)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey50", `TRUE` = "#e12744"),
                    labels = c("r² ≥ 0.95", "r² < 0.95")) +
  labs(x = "Urchin", y = expression(dot(M)*O[2]~"(mg h"^-1*")"), fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

Urchin `h` is flagged, because its 4–29 min window contains the artefact
(Activity 2). Automation makes processing fast and consistent, but it does not
replace looking at the data. Note also that a low r^2^ is not always a sign of a
bad slope (it can simply reflect a low signal-to-noise ratio), so filtering on
r^2^ alone can bias results [@Chabot2021]. Use r^2^ as a prompt to look, not as
an automatic exclusion rule.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 4: Lowest and highest rates in a swim-tunnel trial

`sardine.rd` is a ~2 h swim-tunnel trial on a sardine (*Sardinops sagax*) with
time in seconds and oxygen in **% air saturation**. Metadata: volume 12.3 L,
mass 0.0477 kg, 14.8 °C, salinity 35, 1.013253 bar.

(a) Use `auto_rate()` to find the **lowest** and **highest** rates over a
15-minute window. (b) Convert both to mg O~2~ h^-1^ kg^-1^. (c) What is the ratio
of the highest to the lowest rate? Can you call this an aerobic scope?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 4

```{r}
#| results: hide
#| fig-show: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false
sardine <- inspect(sardine.rd, time = 1, oxygen = 2)

sard_low  <- auto_rate(sardine, method = "lowest",  width = 900, by = "time")
sard_high <- auto_rate(sardine, method = "highest", width = 900, by = "time")

convert_sardine <- function(x) {
  convert_rate(x, oxy.unit = "%Air", time.unit = "sec",
               output.unit = "mg/h/kg", volume = 12.3, mass = 0.0477,
               t = 14.8, S = 35, P = 1.013253)
}
sard_low_conv  <- convert_sardine(sard_low)
sard_high_conv <- convert_sardine(sard_high)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
plot(sard_low, pos = 1)
```

```{r}
sardine_summary <- tibble(
  rate    = c("lowest 15 min", "highest 15 min"),
  mg_h_kg = abs(c(sard_low_conv$rate.output[1], sard_high_conv$rate.output[1]))
)
sardine_summary
sardine_summary$mg_h_kg[2] / sardine_summary$mg_h_kg[1]
```

The highest rate is about
`r round(sardine_summary$mg_h_kg[2] / sardine_summary$mg_h_kg[1], 1)` times the
lowest. This is **not** a proper aerobic scope: the lowest 15-min window in a
2-h trial is not SMR (SMR needs many hours of post-absorptive rest and a
statistical estimator such as a low quantile of many measurements;
@Chabot2016), the highest rate was not produced by an exhaustion protocol, and
both depend strongly on the window width [@Prinzing2021]. Also note that no
background was measured in this dataset, which should be reported.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 5: Intermittent-flow respirometry

`intermittent.rd` contains three closed phases separated by flushes (time in
seconds, O~2~ in mg L^-1^; volume 2.379 L; ash-free dry mass 0.006955 kg). The
closed phases start at rows 1, 2101 and 3901.

Use `calc_rate.int()` to estimate one rate per replicate, ignoring the first
300 s after each closure (`wait`) and measuring over the next 900 s
(`measure`). Convert to mg O~2~ h^-1^ g^-1^ and report the mean ± SD.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 5

```{r}
#| results: hide
#| fig-show: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false
urchin_int <- inspect(intermittent.rd)

int_rates <- calc_rate.int(urchin_int,
                           starts  = c(1, 2101, 3901),
                           wait    = 300,
                           measure = 900)

int_conv <- convert_rate(int_rates,
                         oxy.unit = "mg/L", time.unit = "s",
                         output.unit = "mg/h/g",
                         volume = 2.379, mass = 0.006955)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
plot(int_rates, type = "full")
```

```{r}
summary(int_conv, export = TRUE) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(mean_mg_h_g = mean(abs(rate.output)),
            sd_mg_h_g   = sd(abs(rate.output)),
            n_reps      = n())
```

The `wait` phase excludes the mixing and equilibration period right after the
flush closes, and fixing `measure` gives every replicate the same window
length, which is a reportable, reproducible rule [@Svendsen2016; @Killen2021].
Background respiration was not measured for this dataset, which would need to be
stated in a write-up.
:::

# Aerial

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 6: Activity metabolism

Use `auto_rate()` to find the **highest** 5-min rate in the lizard trial, adjust
it for background, and convert it to mL O~2~ h^-1^ (STPD). How many times higher
is it than the resting rate? When did it occur?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 6

```{r}
#| results: hide
#| fig-show: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false
spec_high <- auto_rate(spec_insp, method = "highest", width = 5, by = "time")
spec_high_conv <- spec_high |>
  adjust_rate(by = blank_rate) |>
  convert_rate(oxy.unit = "umol/L", time.unit = "min",
               output.unit = "umol/h", volume = aerial_meta$air_L)
```

```{r}
#| results: hide
high_df <- summary(spec_high_conv, export = TRUE)
```

```{r}
high_summary <- high_df |>
  as_tibble() |>
  slice(1) |>
  transmute(start_min     = time,
            end_min       = endtime,
            umol_h        = abs(rate.output),
            mL_h_STPD     = umol_h * 22.414 / 1000,
            times_resting = umol_h / aerial_result$umol_h)
high_summary
```

The highest 5-min rate occurred between
`r round(high_summary$start_min, 1)` and `r round(high_summary$end_min, 1)` min,
during the activity burst, and was about
`r round(high_summary$times_resting, 1)` times the resting rate. In a real
study you would confirm activity with video or an activity sensor
[@Wu2024], and note that a burst inside a closed chamber is not a standardised
MMR protocol.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 7: How window width biases "lowest" rates

Many studies estimate SMR as the *lowest* rate over a fixed window. Use
`auto_rate(method = "lowest")` with windows of 5, 10, 15 and 20 min, adjust for
background, and convert to µmol O~2~ h^-1^. Plot the result against window width.
What happens as the window gets shorter, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 7

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
lowest_by_width <- tibble(width_min = c(5, 10, 15, 20)) |>
  mutate(
    rate = map_dbl(width_min, \(w) {
      auto_rate(spec_insp, method = "lowest", width = w, by = "time",
                plot = FALSE)$rate[1]
    }),
    umol_h = abs((rate - blank_rate$rate.bg.mean) * 60 * aerial_meta$air_L)
  )
lowest_by_width
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(lowest_by_width, aes(x = width_min, y = umol_h)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 22.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#e12744") +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 22.5, label = "true resting rate",
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 0, colour = "#e12744") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Window width (min)",
       y = expression("Lowest "*dot(V)*O[2]~"(µmol h"^-1*")")) +
  theme_bw()
```

Shorter windows give *lower* "lowest" rates. With noisy data, each short
regression has a wide sampling error, and searching for the minimum across many
overlapping windows picks the one where noise happened to flatten the slope.
This is the same reason sampling interval changes BMR estimates
[@Hayes1992; @Jacobs2014] and window width changes MMR estimates
[@Prinzing2021]. Choose a window long enough for a precise slope, justify it,
and report it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Activity 8: How big are common mistakes?

Using the resting rate (`spec_rate`) and `blank_rate`, calculate the percentage
error in µmol O~2~ h^-1^ when you:

(a) use the chamber volume (0.150 L) instead of the air volume;
(b) skip the background correction;
(c) convert the hPa trace with `respR`'s water-based units
(`convert_DO(..., from = "hPa", to = "umol/L", S = 0, t = 25)`) instead of the
gas law.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Answer 8

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
correct <- abs((spec_rate$rate - blank_rate$rate.bg.mean) * 60 * aerial_meta$air_L)

err_volume     <- abs((spec_rate$rate - blank_rate$rate.bg.mean) * 60 * aerial_meta$chamber_L)
err_background <- abs(spec_rate$rate * 60 * aerial_meta$air_L)

# (c) treat the gas-phase pO2 as if it were dissolved O2 in water
water_factor <- convert_DO(200, from = "hPa", to = "umol/L", S = 0, t = 25) / 200
gas_factor   <- 1e5 / (R_gas * (25 + 273.15))
err_water    <- correct * water_factor / gas_factor

tibble(mistake   = c("chamber instead of air volume",
                     "no background correction",
                     "water solubility conversion"),
       umol_h    = c(err_volume, err_background, err_water),
       error_pct = round((umol_h / correct - 1) * 100, 1))
```

Forgetting to subtract the animal volume is small here (the lizard is ~3% of
the chamber) but grows with larger animals or smaller chambers. Skipping the
background correction overestimates the rate by roughly the size of the blank
signal. Using water solubility for an air-phase measurement underestimates the
rate about `r round(gas_factor / water_factor)`-fold, an error you would only
catch by sanity-checking against published values.
:::

:::

# Reporting the Workflow {.unnumbered}

Two complementary checklists exist: @Killen2021 for aquatic intermittent-flow
respirometry and @Wu2024 for terrestrial (aerial) respirometry. Both are
organised around the same ideas: describe the **set-up**, the **animals**, the
**measurement conditions**, the **data processing** and the **statistics**, and
share data and code [@Parker2018; @Whitlock2011]. For the processing steps
covered here, report:

| Step | Report | Where it lives in `respR` |
|----|----|----|
| Data acquisition | Sensor/analyser type and model, sampling interval, calibration | Your metadata |
| Quality control | Data excluded and why (artefacts, activity, drop-outs) | `inspect()` plots, your code |
| Rate extraction | Method (manual window, `auto_rate()` method), window width, wait/measure phases, number of slopes used, any r^2^ criterion | `$summary` (`time`, `endtime`, `rsq`) |
| Background | How and when measured, how applied, its size relative to animal rates | `adjust_rate()` (`adjustment`) |
| Conversion | Units, effective volume, mass (and how measured), t, S, P, STP definition, equations used | `convert_rate()` (`volume`, `mass`, `S`, `t`, `P`) |
| Final metric | SMR/RMR/MMR definition and estimator | Your code |
| Software | R and package versions, citations | `sessionInfo()`, `citation()` |
| Data and code | Raw traces + processing scripts + README/metadata in a public repository | Dryad, Zenodo, OSF, Figshare |


A methods paragraph can be generated directly from the analysis objects, so the
text always matches the numbers:

> Oxygen uptake of urchin *n* was calculated in R (`r R.version.string`) with
> `respR` v`r packageVersion("respR")` [@Harianto2019] as the slope of a linear
> regression of oxygen concentration against time between
> `r urch_final_df$time` and `r urch_final_df$endtime` min (r^2^ =
> `r round(urch_final_df$rsq, 3)`), adjusted for the mean background rate of two
> blank chambers (`r signif(urch_final_df$adjustment, 3)` mg L^-1^ min^-1^), and
> converted to `r urch_final_df$output.unit` using an effective volume of
> `r urch_final_df$volume` L and a mass of `r urch_final_df$mass` kg.

# Caveats {.unnumbered}

- **Linearity is an assumption.** Rates assume a linear decline within the
  window. Curvature from mixing lag, sensor response time or falling O~2~
  violates this; keep closed-phase O~2~ high (often > 80% air saturation) unless
  hypoxia is the treatment [@Svendsen2016].
- **Temperature control.** Rates are only interpretable at a stable, reported
  temperature; in air, temperature changes also change $p\text{O}_2$ directly.
- **Effective volume** must include tubing and exclude the animal; errors scale
  linearly into the final rate.
- **Background** changes over time and with feeding or biofilm; measure it more
  than once and report how it was modelled [@Killen2021].
- **Window width and selection rules** (lowest, highest, quantiles, r^2^
  filters) systematically change estimates; justify and report them
  [@Hayes1992; @Chabot2021; @Prinzing2021].
- **SMR needs time and replication.** Use long trials, many slopes and an
  established estimator (e.g. a low quantile or the mean of the lowest normal
  distribution) rather than a single lowest slope [@Chabot2016].
- **Animal state.** Handling stress, digestion, time of day, activity,
  reproductive state and acclimation all affect MR; record and report them
  [@Wu2024].
- **Unit conversions in `respR` are aquatic.** For gas-phase data, convert with
  the gas law, account for water vapour and CO~2~ where fractions are measured,
  and define STP [@Withers2001; @Lighton2019; @Wu2024].
- **Mass-specific rates** remove the effect of mass only when MR scales
  isometrically; model mass as a covariate instead of dividing by it
  [@Packard1988; @Wu2024].
- **Sanity-check every new dataset** against published values for similar
  species, sizes and temperatures.

When using `respR`, please cite @Harianto2019. If you have raw oxygen traces
that are not yet supported, contact the package maintainer, Nicholas Carey.
